why: Closing and reckoning items mix celebration and thanks with reports of the final state, so T3-009 and T3-073 are easy to swap.

why.T3-065: The concepts call the room to make, size, place, correct and join the Uruguay flag itself; the flag of the room's land is T3-065 rather than generic calls/templates or design talk.

why.T3-054: The single concept recruits people to build the Uruguay flag on an unofficial sequel after the original canvas closed, which is carrying the work to a later canvas.

why.T3-021: The concepts sign up for upkeep, call repairs, give repair coordinates, rebuild periodically, and fix or relocate the damaged heart; this is watching and repairing the work rather than fighting an attack.

why.T3-072: The concepts thank Bulgarian allies and other neighbours, recount who helped and how the alliance began, and return thanks; this is thanking allies rather than celebrating the room's own work or forming a new alliance.

why.T3-105: The concepts make, request, deliver and thank for a fixed image or version of the group's r/place work, including a Bulgarian-flag version; this is saving and circulating a final image record rather than in-canvas repair or a new canvas.

why.T3-117: Both concepts register that placement or the canvas has ended; they mark the canvas's end rather than celebrating the finished work or reporting its history.

why.T3-031: The single concept is a meme or catchphrase about comments in the room's talk; it plays the room's in-joke rather than explaining the canvas or directing placements.

why.T3-009: The concepts close the effort with WE DID IT and thanks for participation; the room's achieved result is celebrated, with the end notice subordinate.
The concepts celebrate completing and maintaining the Uruguay designs, thank participants for the 72-hour push, and frame it as an achievement for a tiny sub; this is celebrating the finished work.

why.T3-073: The concepts report and reckon with what happened to the final cubes: wrong at the end, good minutes earlier, holding the void at bay, and late maintenance, so this is reporting how the work fared rather than simply mourning or celebrating.

why.T3-117: Both concepts register that placement or the canvas has ended; they mark the canvas's end rather than celebrating the finished work or reporting its history.

why.T3-151: The concepts organise reciprocal help with Argentina, Brazil and other neighbours: posting for aid and returning it, trading help through Discord, maintaining flags together, and limiting expansion because helpers would be harmed; this is bartering help rather than a one-way ask or a chat meeting.

why.T3-029: The concepts mourn an unfinished heart and recount the loss of a lower heart to Greece; this is grief for the room's lost or unfinished work.

why.T3-010: The concepts negotiate and contest space with neighbours: agreeing with another builder, taking or redirecting hearts from Greece, China and Pansexual Pride, and calling to take Serbia's space, which is settling borders and space with neighbours.
why.T3-113: Distinct concepts add Uruguay's national emblems and words to the corner: writing URUGUAY below the flag, activating Capitán Yorugua with local icons, finishing URUGUAY before flag, mate and thermos, and loving the mate while wishing for a thermos.

multiplacement_log.why_not_one: T3-010 can carry the boundary and neighbour negotiations over hearts and Serbia's space, but it does not carry the material about adding Uruguay's national words and icons to the corner.
multiplacement_log.why_this_one: C0696574 writes URUGUAY below the flag, C1477226 activates Capitán Yorugua with local icons, C1372789 prioritizes the URUGUAY word before flag, mate and thermos, and C0019505 wishes for mate and thermos; these satisfy T3-113's gate for national emblems and words added beside the flag.
multiplacement_log.dispensable: T3-113; dropping it would lose the national emblems and words being decided into Uruguay's corner.

why.T3-006: The concepts call cubers to nuke others on a second Place mosaic; this is calling for attacks that deface others' work rather than simply carrying work to a new canvas.
